storm.summary_layperson: No thunderstorm risk tonight — it's mostly sunny and dry, with any building storm threat holding off until midweek.
storm.local_effect_blurb: There's nothing on radar to test the Sound's cooling effect right now, so the marine layer isn't a factor tonight.
storm.detail_html:
Radar (KOKX) shows no storm cells anywhere near the cove, there are no active NWS alerts, and model instability (CAPE) is reading 0 J/kg — there's essentially no fuel for thunderstorms this evening.

The Sound's cooling marine layer is present but not being tested: water is running about 74°F against air near 82°F, an 8–9°F air–water difference that would normally build a moderate stabilizing layer over the water. With no storms approaching, that mechanism is simply idle tonight rather than actively protecting or amplifying anything.

The New York/Long Island (OKX) forecast discussion does flag an increasing threat: as the region sits on the northwest edge of a building Bermuda ridge, scattered afternoon and evening thunderstorms return Wednesday and continue into the weekend, with an isolated severe and flash-flood risk once moisture builds later in the week.

For tonight's 17:00–22:00 window specifically: expect a quiet, sunny evening with no storm impact on the wind window. What would change the call: any new convective development showing up on radar, or an updated AFD pulling that Wednesday threat earlier.

wind.tactics_blurb: A light, patchy sea breeze fills in from the SE backing toward S/SSW through the evening, but it's marginal — expect drifter conditions, favor the left/west side of the course, and don't expect much wind left after sunset (~8:07 PM).
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a sea-breeze day, but a weak one: the air–water temperature difference is 8.5°F (comfortably above the 5°F threshold for thermal potential), and the background gradient wind is calm-to-light out of the NE (~5 mph per NWS), which doesn't oppose the sea breeze. That combination puts today in thermal-day territory rather than a gradient-only day — but the sea-breeze signal itself is thin: only 38% of CT-coast stations are showing southerly flow, and direction agreement across the regional station ensemble is just 0.41, both signs of a patchy, immature sea breeze rather than a robust, well-established one.

At the cove, RYC is currently reading SE 2.8 kt (10-min avg 2.6, gust 4.5) — light and consistent with a marginal thermal. HRRR's raw forecast direction (SSE ~150°) is running about 6° behind the live western-LIS obs (SE ~144°), a small enough gap that we're not fully overriding the model, but the standard sea-breeze maturation veer (+15°) has been applied to the forecast hours above, carrying the direction from SSE early in the window toward S/SSW by 19:00–20:00 as the breeze (such as it is) matures.

Per the cove geography table, S–SE flow favors the west shore of the course — the east side near Tod's Point sits in partial shelter and will be lighter and shiftier. Favor the left/west side on the beat.

Shift character is the ramping-to-mature transition: expect a gradual persistent veer (SE → S → SSW) rather than clean oscillations, since the SB never fully matures into a strong, stable thermal today.

Racers should expect 2–6 kt through the window — drifter-class, finicky conditions for one-designs, with real risk the breeze goes fully light and variable once the thermal collapses around sunset (8:07 PM). Don't expect a strong evening thermal to bail out a slow start; if the fleet isn't moving by mid-window, it likely won't get much better.

data_caveats: Buoy 44040 / WLIS_MET reading is 75–87 minutes old — sea-breeze depth and SST inputs are slightly stale.
Sea-breeze signal is weak and patchy today (38% of CT-coast stations southerly, direction agreement 0.41) — treat wind timing and direction as lower-confidence than a mature sea-breeze day.
